## Summary

Drummatick shares Peter Steinberger's result: **OpenClaw ran a test-audit skill and deleted around 400k lines of its own tests with little change in code coverage.** Steinberger's diagnosis: modern models love writing tests for every tiny change even when they aren't useful — tests as output-slop, not as verification. The skill (now in OpenClaw's repo) audits the test suite and flags/deletes the ones that don't pay for themselves.

## Why it matters

- **The quantified version of "tests that repeat the code back."** [[2026-09-26-pocock-retro-pr-talk]] (same capture batch) has Pocock/Opus-5 naming the behavior; Steinberger's 400k-LOC number is what it costs when it goes unchecked. Together they close the loop: name the failure → measure the pile → ship the audit skill.
- **Second drummatick share in the vault, same shape as the first.** [[2026-08-30-cyclomatic-complexity-skill]] was a mechanical complexity gate; this one is a *deletion* gate. Both are "small guardrail beats big framework" ([[2026-09-14-rauchg-verifiers-skills-new-frameworks]]) — one catches slop at write-time, the other audits it away after the fact. A mature harness plausibly wants both directions.
- **Directly relevant to this company's own artifact hygiene.** Our tasks leave behind check scripts, one-off .mjs helpers, and test scaffolding that accrete exactly the way OpenClaw's tests did. The mirror of [[2026-09-26-pocock-coding-standards-accretion]]: standards should accrete from failures, but *artifacts* should be audited down — the failure mode of an agent company is unbounded scaffolding that nobody deletes.
- **Skepticism gates:** "not much change in code coverage" is Steinberger's claim, not a verified number — coverage is a weak proxy (tests that assert nothing also "count" the same as real ones, so even that metric can't tell you what was lost). n=1 repo, n=1 audit run, no false-deletion data. The skill sits in OpenClaw's repo, so it's tuned to their harness, not a drop-in for ours.
